response.text:
The family of Dashwood had long been settled in Sussex. Their estate was large, and their residence at Norland Park, where for many generations they had lived so respectably as to engage the general good opinion of their acquaintance. The late owner, a single man of very advanced age, had long had his sister as companion and housekeeper; her death, ten years before his own, altered his home so much that, to supply her loss, he invited into his house the family of his nephew, Mr. Henry Dashwood, the legal inheritor of Norland, and the person to whom he intended to bequeath it. In their society he was comfortable; his attachment to them all increased; Mr. and Mrs. Henry Dashwood’s attentions gave him solid comfort, and the cheerfulness of the children added a relish to his existence.

By a former marriage, Mr. Henry Dashwood had one son; by his present lady, three daughters. The son, a steady respectable young man, was amply provided for by his mother’s large fortune, half of which devolved on him at his coming of age; by his own marriage he added to his wealth. To him, therefore, the succession to Norland was not so important as to his sisters; for their fortune, independent of what might arise from their father’s inheritance, could be but small. Their mother had nothing; their father had only seven thousand pounds in his own disposal; the remaining moiety of his first wife’s fortune was secured to her child, and he had only a life-interest in it.

The old gentleman died; his will was read, and, like almost every other will, gave as much disappointment as pleasure. He was not unjust enough to leave his estate from his nephew;—but he left it on such terms as destroyed half the value. It was secured to Mr. Dashwood’s son, and to his son’s son, a child of four years old, in such a way as to leave to Mr. Dashwood no power of providing for those most dear to him by any charge on the estate, or by any sale of its valuable woods. The whole was tied up for the benefit of this child, who, in occasional visits, had gained on his uncle’s affections by such attractions as are by no means unusual in children of two or three years old; an imperfect articulation, an earnest desire of having his own way, many cunning tricks, and a great deal of noise. As a mark of affection for the three girls, he left them a thousand pounds a-piece.

Mr. Dashwood’s temper was cheerful and sanguine; he hoped to live to improve the estate and lay by a sum; but he survived his uncle no longer. Ten thousand pounds, including the legacies, was all that remained to his widow and daughters.

His son was sent for; to him Mr. Dashwood recommended, with all the urgency which illness could command, the interest of his mother-in-law and sisters. Mr. John Dashwood was affected, and promised to do every thing in his power. He had then leisure to consider how much there might prudently be in his power to do. He was not an ill-disposed young man, unless to be rather cold hearted and rather selfish is to be ill-disposed; well respected, conducting himself with propriety. Had he married a more amiable woman, he might even have been made amiable himself; but Mrs. John Dashwood was a strong caricature of himself;—more narrow-minded and selfish. He meditated to increase his sisters’ fortunes by a present of a thousand pounds a-piece; then, warmed by the prospect of income, “Yes, he would give them three thousand pounds: it would be liberal and handsome! ... Three thousand pounds!”

No sooner was his father’s funeral over, than Mrs. John Dashwood, without notice to her mother-in-law, arrived with her child and attendants. No one could dispute her right; but the indelicacy was the greater; and in _her_ mind there was a sense of honor so keen, a generosity so romantic, that any offence of the kind was a source of immovable disgust. She would have quitted the house for ever, had not the entreaty of her eldest girl induced reflection, and her love for all her children determined her to stay, and avoid a breach with their brother.

Elinor, this eldest daughter, possessed a strength of understanding and coolness of judgment which, though only nineteen, qualified her to be her mother’s counsellor, and to counteract that eagerness of mind in Mrs. Dashwood which must generally have led to imprudence. She had an excellent heart;—her disposition affectionate, her feelings strong; but she knew how to govern them: a knowledge her mother had yet to learn; and which one sister had resolved never to be taught.

Marianne’s abilities were, in many respects, quite equal to Elinor’s. She was sensible and clever; but eager in everything: generous, amiable, interesting; she was everything but prudent. The resemblance between her and her mother was strikingly great. Elinor saw, with concern, the excess of her sister’s sensibility; by Mrs. Dashwood it was valued and cherished. They encouraged each other in the violence of their affliction; renewed and created their sorrow. Elinor, too, was deeply afflicted; but still she could consult with her brother, receive her sister-in-law with proper attention, and strive to rouse her mother to similar exertion.

Margaret, the other sister, was good-humored and well-disposed; but having imbibed much of Marianne’s romance without much of her sense, did not, at thirteen, bid fair to equal her sisters.
